pll1d8c1-d1e3476.summary: Announces the new topic: the truth or propriety, immutability, and simplicity of the divine nature, substance, or essence.

pll1d8c1-d1e3479.summary: With De Trinitate V, God is undoubtedly substance or, better, essence (ousia), named from 'to be' as wisdom is from 'to be wise.' None is more than the one who said 'I am who am.' He is truly and properly essence, whose essence knows no past or future.
claims: God is substance or, more fittingly, essence.
Essence is named from esse.
God is truly and properly essence, without past or future.

pll1d8c1-d1e3511.summary: Cites Jerome: God alone, without beginning, holds the name of true essence. Compared with him who truly is because unchangeable, changeable things are as if they were not. What 'was' no longer is and what 'will be' is not yet, but God only is.
claims: Only God truly is, because he is unchangeable.
Changeable things are as nothing compared to God.
God knows no 'was' or 'will be.'

pll1d8c1-d1e3533.summary: Raises a difficulty about Jerome's words, since Scripture says God was from eternity and will be forever. Saying only 'was' might suggest he ceased, only 'is' that he began, only 'will be' that he is not now; so it is better to say he always was, is, and will be.
claims: God always was, is, and will be.
Using only one tense of God could suggest beginning or ending.

pll1d8c1-d1e3549.summary: Cites Augustine on John: 'is' is properly said of the eternal, but by our manner we rightly say 'was' (never ceased) and 'will be' (never lacking). Verbs of every tense are truly said of him who never was absent, as with the Spirit who 'will hear,' whose hearing is knowing and being, received from the one from whom he proceeds.
claims: 'Is' is properly said of the eternal.
Verbs of any tense are truly said of God.
In the Spirit, to hear is to know, which is to be.
The Spirit receives essence and knowledge from the one from whom he proceeds.

pll1d8c1-d1e3586.summary: Resolves Jerome's dictum: although substantive verbs of different tenses are said of God, they do not mark temporal passage but signify the existence of the Godhead simply. So God alone is properly called essence or being.
claims: Tensed verbs said of God signify his existence simply, without temporal motion.
God alone is properly called essence or being.

pll1d8c1-d1e3594.summary: Adds Hilary: being is not an accident to God but subsisting truth, abiding cause, and the natural property of his kind.
claims: Being is not an accident in God.
God's being is subsisting truth and abiding cause.

pl-l1d8c1.summary: Opens the treatment of the truth or propriety, immutability, and simplicity of the divine essence. With Augustine, God is essence (ousia), named from 'to be,' as revealed in 'I am who am,' and alone is truly and properly essence, without past or future (Jerome). Lombard then explains Jerome's 'God only is and knows no was or will be': Scripture also says God was and will be, and Augustine allows verbs of every tense of God; what is meant is that such verbs signify not temporal motion but the simple existence of the Godhead. So God alone is properly called essence or being, and being is not an accident in him (Hilary).
claims: God is essence, named from 'to be,' as the name 'I am who am' shows.
God alone is truly and properly essence, since his being has no past or future.
Compared with God's being, the being of mutable things is as nothing.
Verbs of every tense may be said of God, but 'is' properly.
Tensed verbs predicated of God signify his existence simply, without temporal motion.
Being is not an accident in God.
